cards.q: What is meant by the rate of a reaction?
cards.a: The change in concentration (or amount) of a reactant or product per unit time.
cards.why: Measured as concentration change per second, the unit is \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}\).

cards.q: Give three ways of following the rate of a reaction that gives off a gas, such as marble chips with hydrochloric acid.
cards.a: Measure the volume of gas with a gas syringe; measure the loss in mass as gas escapes (on a balance); or time how long the reaction takes to finish.
cards.why: Each gives a measurable quantity that changes with time as the reaction proceeds.

cards.q: 48 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of carbon dioxide is collected in the first 30 s of a reaction. Calculate the mean rate of gas production over this time.
cards.a: 1.6 \(\text{cm}^{3}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)
cards.why: This is a mean rate over 30 s; the rate at any instant is found from a tangent.

cards.q: In the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid, a cross under the flask disappears after 40 s. What value can be used as a measure of the rate?
cards.a: \(0.025\ \text{s}^{-1}\)
steps: The same amount of sulfur forms each time the cross disappears, so rate \(\propto \frac{1}{t}\).
cards.why: A longer time means a slower reaction, so 1/time is used as a relative rate.

cards.q: How do you find the rate at a particular time from a concentration–time graph? How do you find the initial rate?
cards.a: Draw a tangent to the curve at that time and calculate its gradient (change in y ÷ change in x). For the initial rate, draw the tangent at t = 0.
cards.why: Use a long tangent and read two points far apart on it to keep the gradient accurate. The rate is the size of the gradient.

cards.q: A tangent drawn to a graph of reactant concentration against time at t = 30 s passes through (0 s, 0.080 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)) and (60 s, 0.020 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)). Calculate the rate at 30 s.
cards.a: \(1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)
steps: The concentration of reactant falls, so the gradient is negative; rate \(= 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}\).
cards.why: A rate is always quoted as a positive value.

cards.q: On a graph of volume of hydrogen against time, the tangent drawn at t = 0 passes through (0 s, 0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\)) and (20 s, 50 \(\text{cm}^{3}\)). Calculate the initial rate.
cards.a: 2.5 \(\text{cm}^{3}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)
steps: Initial rate \(=\) gradient of the tangent at \(t = 0\)
cards.why: The initial rate is the fastest rate, because reactant concentrations are highest at the start.

cards.q: Marble chips react with hydrochloric acid in a flask on a balance. The mass falls by 0.88 g in the first 60 s. Calculate the mean rate of formation of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) in \(\text{mol s}^{-1}\). (\(M_{\text{r}}\) \(\mathrm{CO_{2}} = 44.0\))
cards.a: \(3.3 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol s}^{-1}\)
steps: The mass lost is the carbon dioxide that escaped: \(n = \frac{0.88}{44.0} = 0.020\ \text{mol}\)
cards.why: A cotton wool plug in the neck of the flask lets the gas out but stops acid spray escaping, which would add to the mass loss.

cards.q: A graph of volume of gas against time is steepest at the start and then levels off. Explain its shape.
cards.a: The rate is fastest at the start and falls to zero as a reactant is used up.
marks: At the start the concentration of reactants is highest, so collisions are most frequent and the rate is highest.
As reactants are used up, the concentration falls, so there are fewer collisions per second and the gradient decreases.
The line becomes horizontal when the limiting reactant is used up: the reaction has stopped.

cards.q: According to collision theory, what is needed for a reaction to occur between two particles?
cards.a: The particles must collide, and the collision must have at least the activation energy.
cards.why: They must also collide with a suitable orientation, so that the right bonds can break.

cards.q: Define activation energy.
cards.a: The minimum energy that particles need when they collide for a reaction to occur, \(E_{\text{a}}\).
cards.why: It is the energy needed to start breaking bonds.

cards.q: Explain why most collisions between particles do not lead to a reaction.
cards.a: Most colliding particles do not have enough energy.
marks: Only collisions with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy can lead to reaction.
Most particles have energies below the activation energy, so most collisions are unsuccessful.
Particles may also collide with the wrong orientation.

cards.q: On a reaction profile (enthalpy against progress of reaction), how are the activation energy and the enthalpy change shown?
cards.a:
\(E_{\text{a}}\): the height from the energy of the reactants up to the top of the peak.
\(\Delta H\): the difference in energy between the reactants and the products.
cards.why: For an exothermic reaction the products are below the reactants (\(\Delta H\) negative); for an endothermic reaction they are above.

cards.q: What does a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution show, and what are its axes?
cards.a:
The spread of energies of the molecules in a gas at a given temperature.
x-axis: energy. y-axis: number (or fraction) of molecules with that energy.
cards.why: Molecules in a gas do not all have the same energy, because they constantly collide and exchange energy.

cards.q: Describe the key features of a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve.
cards.a: It starts at the origin; rises to a peak at the most probable energy; has a long tail on the high-energy side; and never meets the energy axis.
cards.why: No molecules have zero energy, there is no maximum energy, and the area under the curve equals the total number of molecules.

cards.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, where are the most probable energy and the mean energy?
cards.a: The most probable energy is at the peak. The mean energy is slightly to the right of the peak.
cards.why: The curve is not symmetrical: its long high-energy tail pulls the mean above the most probable value.

cards.q: How does the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve change when the temperature of the same gas sample is increased?
cards.a: The peak moves to the right (higher energy) and is lower; the curve is broader; the area under it is unchanged.
cards.why: The number of molecules is the same, so the area stays the same; more of the area now lies beyond the activation energy.

cards.q: How does the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve change when the temperature is lowered?
cards.a: The peak is higher and moves to the left (lower energy); the area is unchanged.
cards.why: Fewer molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so the rate is lower.

cards.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, how is the number of molecules able to react shown?
cards.a: Mark the activation energy, \(E_{\text{a}}\), on the energy axis. The area under the curve to the right of \(E_{\text{a}}\) is the number of molecules with enough energy to react.
cards.why: Comparing this area at two temperatures, or with and without a catalyst, explains the change in rate.

cards.q: Use the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution to explain why a small increase in temperature causes a large increase in the rate of reaction.
cards.a: Many more molecules have energy at or above the activation energy.
marks: At a higher temperature the distribution shifts to higher energies.
A much larger proportion of molecules have energy \(\geq E_{\text{a}}\) (larger area to the right of \(E_{\text{a}}\)).
So a much larger proportion of collisions are successful.
Collisions are also slightly more frequent, but this is a much smaller effect.

cards.q: True or false: raising the temperature increases the rate mainly because particles collide more often.
cards.a: False. The main reason is that a much larger proportion of collisions have energy at or above the activation energy.
cards.why: Collision frequency rises only slightly with temperature; the number of molecules beyond the activation energy rises sharply.

cards.q: True or false: increasing the temperature lowers the activation energy.
cards.a: False. The activation energy is unchanged; more molecules have energy above it.
cards.why: Only a catalyst (a different route) changes the activation energy.

cards.q: Explain why increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increases the rate of reaction.
cards.a: There are more frequent collisions, so more successful collisions per second.
marks: There are more particles in the same volume.
So collisions occur more frequently.
So there are more collisions with energy at or above the activation energy per unit time.

cards.q: Explain why increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction increases its rate.
cards.a: The same number of gas molecules are in a smaller volume.
marks: Higher pressure means more gas molecules per unit volume (a higher concentration).
So collisions occur more frequently.
So there are more successful collisions per unit time.

cards.q: True or false: increasing concentration increases the rate because a greater proportion of collisions are successful.
cards.a: False. The proportion of successful collisions is the same; there are simply more collisions per second.
cards.why: Concentration does not change the energies of the molecules: only temperature (or a catalyst) changes the proportion with enough energy.

cards.q: Explain why powdered marble reacts faster with hydrochloric acid than the same mass of marble chips.
cards.a: The powder has a larger surface area.
marks: Powder has a larger surface area exposed to the acid.
More particles are available on the surface to collide with acid particles.
So collisions, and successful collisions, are more frequent.

cards.q: Excess hydrochloric acid reacts with 1 g of marble chips and, separately, with 1 g of powdered marble. How do the two graphs of volume of CO₂ against time compare?
cards.a: The powder’s curve is steeper at the start and levels off sooner, but both level off at the same final volume.
cards.why: The marble is the limiting reactant and the same mass is used, so the same amount of carbon dioxide forms.

cards.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of thiosulfate ions with acid that is used to study rates.
cards.why: The sulfur forms a pale yellow precipitate that gradually hides a cross drawn under the flask.

cards.q: Outline how to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid.
cards.a: Warm the thiosulfate solution in a water bath to a set temperature and measure it. Add the acid, start a timer and time how long until a cross under the flask can no longer be seen. Repeat at several temperatures with the same volumes and concentrations. Plot 1/time (the rate) against temperature.
cards.why: Only the temperature is changed; volumes, concentrations, the flask and the cross are kept the same.

cards.q: Suggest improvements and a safety precaution for the thiosulfate “disappearing cross” experiment.
cards.a: Reduce errors in timing and temperature; avoid breathing sulfur dioxide.
marks: Measure the temperature of the mixture at the start and end and use the mean.
Use the same person, the same cross and the same depth of solution to judge the end point.
Use a light sensor or colorimeter to detect the end point instead of the eye.
Sulfur dioxide is toxic: work in a well-ventilated room and dispose of the mixture promptly.

cards.q: Use collision theory to explain why food keeps longer in a fridge and why beans cook faster in a pressure cooker.
cards.a: In a fridge the lower temperature slows the reactions that spoil food. In a pressure cooker water boils above 100 °C, so the cooking reactions are faster.
cards.why: At a higher temperature a greater proportion of molecules have energy at or above the activation energy, and vice versa.

cards.q: What is a catalyst?
cards.a: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being changed in chemical composition or amount at the end.
cards.why: Because it is not used up, a small amount of catalyst can be used again and again.

cards.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
cards.a: It provides an alternative reaction route (pathway) with a lower activation energy.
cards.why: More collisions then have energy at or above the new, lower activation energy.

cards.q: Use a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution to explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a gaseous reaction.
cards.a: The activation energy is lower, so more molecules have enough energy to react.
marks: The catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy.
The distribution curve itself is unchanged (same temperature).
The lower \(E_{\text{a}}\) is further to the left, so a larger area lies to its right: more molecules have energy \(\geq E_{\text{a}}\).
So a greater proportion of collisions are successful and the rate increases.

cards.q: True or false: adding a catalyst moves the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve to the right.
cards.a: False. The curve does not change; only the activation energy is marked further to the left.
cards.why: The curve depends only on temperature. A catalyst changes the route, not the energies of the molecules.

cards.q: Describe the reaction profiles for the same exothermic reaction with and without a catalyst.
cards.a: Both start at the same reactant energy and finish at the same product energy. The catalysed route has a lower peak (lower activation energy).
cards.why: The enthalpy change, \(\Delta H\), is the same: a catalyst does not change the energies of the reactants or products.

cards.q: True or false: a catalyst makes a reaction more exothermic.
cards.a: False. \(\Delta H\) is unchanged; only the activation energy is lowered.
cards.why: The reactants and products are the same, so the overall energy change is the same.

cards.q: Explain how a solid (heterogeneous) catalyst speeds up a reaction between gases.
cards.a: It provides a surface on which the reaction happens.
marks: Reactant molecules are adsorbed onto the catalyst surface (at active sites).
Bonds in the reactants are weakened, and the molecules are held close together, so they react more easily.
The products are desorbed, freeing the surface for more reactant molecules.

cards.q: Why is a solid catalyst used in industry as a fine powder, a mesh or a coating on a support?
cards.a: To give it a very large surface area, so more reactant molecules can be adsorbed at once and the rate is greater.
cards.why: An example is the iron catalyst in the Haber process, \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\); catalytic converters spread platinum, palladium and rhodium thinly over a ceramic honeycomb.

cards.q: Explain the economic benefits of using catalysts in industrial processes.
cards.a: Catalysts let products be made faster and with less energy.
marks: An acceptable rate is reached at a lower temperature, so less energy (fuel) is needed and costs are lower.
Product is made faster, so more is produced per day from the same plant.
The catalyst is not used up, so it can be reused for a long time.
Burning less fuel also means lower carbon dioxide emissions.

cards.q: List the factors that affect the rate of a reaction, and say which of them change the proportion of collisions that are successful.
cards.a:
Concentration, pressure (gases), surface area (solids), temperature and catalysts.
Only temperature and a catalyst change the proportion of successful collisions; the others change how often collisions happen.
cards.why: Temperature changes the energies of the molecules; a catalyst lowers the energy needed.
